messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Prosecutor
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 50

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no bullet points.

Raúl had spent most of his adult life presenting himself as composed, exacting, and hard to shake. As a prosecutor in a busy county office, he was used to confrontation, detail, and long hours spent listening to other people’s worst moments. He had built a reputation for being steady under pressure, the kind of man who could walk into a courtroom early, coffee in hand, and organize an entire case from memory. Since his wife died three years ago, however, that steadiness had become more of a performance than a feeling. He lived alone in the same modest house in a largely Latino neighborhood where he and his wife had raised their two children, and he kept himself occupied with work, church on Sundays, and short visits from his granddaughter. He rarely spoke about his own distress, in part because he believed that at his age he should be able to manage it and in part because he felt a deep shame that made the whole experience feel unspeakable.

The assault happened after a late evening deposition, when Raúl accepted a drink with a colleague at a downtown hotel bar. He remembered feeling tired and relieved to be off the clock, then increasingly foggy after only one drink, which was unusual for him. The last clear memory he has is of standing near the elevator, trying to make a joke, and then of waking later with pain, disorientation, and the certainty that something had been done to him while he was too impaired to stop it. He did not report it right away. He showered repeatedly, scrubbed his body, and threw away the clothes he had been wearing. For days he told himself that maybe he had misunderstood, that maybe he had simply been drugged and robbed, because the alternative felt unbearable. Yet the physical memories were there, along with flashes of a man’s weight pinning him down and a sense of helplessness that left him nauseated. He began sleeping in fragments, waking with his heart pounding and his body tense, as if he were bracing for another blow.

Over the following weeks, Raúl became increasingly preoccupied with what had happened. He found himself replaying the evening in involuntary snippets, often while driving or sitting in court, and these images would arrive with a sudden rush of heat, panic, and disgust. The hotel lobby, the smell of cologne in an elevator, the sound of keys jingling, and even the metallic taste of certain drinks could pull him back into the memory with vivid force. He started avoiding the downtown district altogether, sending junior attorneys to hearings there when he could, and he made excuses to skip after-work gatherings. At the office he became guarded about being alone with male colleagues, especially in enclosed spaces like conference rooms or elevators, because he feared being trapped and humiliated again. He told himself that caution was rational, that a man in his position could not afford to be careless, but his avoidance gradually narrowed his world.

Raúl also began to see himself differently. Before the assault he had trusted his judgment and taken pride in being a strong, competent man. Afterward he felt contaminated and weak, as though the event had exposed a failure in him that others would eventually detect. He was ashamed that he had not fought harder, and ashamed that, as a heterosexual man who had spent his life working in a masculine profession, he now felt so shaken by something he believed he should have been able to shrug off. At times he wondered whether the assault meant he was somehow less of a man, and that thought deepened his isolation. He stopped reaching out to friends, declined invitations to family dinners, and became irritable with his children when they asked why he seemed distracted. His nights were the worst: he would check locks twice, keep the television on for background noise, and lie stiffly in bed, listening for sounds in the house. He slept poorly and woke unrefreshed, with a startle response so pronounced that the phone ringing or a voice behind him in the hallway could leave him shaking.

Over the months, Raúl also noticed a persistent bitterness and grief that he could not easily name. He felt detached from others, unable to enjoy his work in the way he once had, and increasingly certain that the world was unsafe and that people, even familiar ones, could not be trusted. He interpreted his own distress as proof that he was failing at both strength and dignity. Although he continued to function outwardly, he was doing so through constant effort: arriving early to arrange his desk near the door, scanning public spaces for exits, avoiding after-hours solitude, and pushing away intrusive images whenever they surfaced. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent incident in the courthouse garage, where the sound of footsteps approaching behind him triggered such a surge of fear and physical panic that he had to sit in his car for nearly twenty minutes before he could drive home. He realized then that his efforts to manage on his own were no longer enough. He came to treatment hoping to regain sleep and control, but more than that, he was afraid that if he kept living this way he would become permanently trapped in the humiliation and fear of that night.
